extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, literary critics, and serious readers of drama/poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating dramatic and poetic works (style, plotting, characterization, and editorial/textual fidelity), drawn from close readings of Renaissance and early modern dramatists. Useful for playwrights, critics, and editors seeking principles of effective dramatic writing and editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poem must be music or sense
rubrics_metrics.description: "To please me, a poem must be either music or sense; if it is neither, I confess I cannot interest myself in it.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem should excel either in its aural qualities (rhythm, melody, musical phrasing) or in intellectual/contentual clarity and meaning. If it lacks both, it will fail to engage. Use musical devices or strong sense/argument to carry the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue can outweigh artificial plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Beaumont and Fletcher's plots are 'wholly inartificial; they only care to pitch a character into a position to make him or her talk; you must swallow all their gross improbabilities, and, taking it all for granted, attend only to the dialogue.',
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In plays where plotting is loose or improbable, the success depends on vivid, persuasive dialogue and character speech. Writers may intentionally permit improbable premises if the dialogue justifies and sustains audience interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent conception and execution of comic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters like Lawrit are 'conceived and executed from first to last in genuine comic humour.',
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comic character should be consistently and fully realized across all scenes — conception (idea) and execution (performance/lines) must align to preserve humorous effect and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial fidelity and textual restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of poor modern editions and the claim that many passages 'could with certainty [be] put back into their original verse, and more that could be replaced in their native prose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should respect original forms (verse/prose), restore corrupted passages when possible, and avoid negligent alterations; careful textual scholarship enhances the integrity and reader's experience of older plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek universality rather than mannered imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspeare is 'universal, and, in fact, has no manner'; attempts to imitate his style tend to produce the mannerisms of other dramatists instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a voice that expresses universal human truth rather than adopting recognizable 'mannerisms' of a single master. Imitation often reveals other influences; strive for individual universality and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural sentence progression and inwoven meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: "In Shakspeare one sentence begets the next naturally; the meaning is all inwoven. He goes on kindling like a meteor..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose sentences and lines so each follows organically from the previous one; ensure tightly woven meaning and logical/emotional momentum rather than disjointed or forced transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bold villains to voice risky opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspeare 'always makes of his bold villains...vehicles for expressing opinions and conjectures of a nature too hazardous for a wise man to put forth directly as his own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex antagonists can be a safe dramatic mouthpiece for controversial or unsettling ideas; use them to explore viewpoints the 'author' cannot state directly without breaking character plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance diction between colloquial and elevated registers
rubrics_metrics.description: "The styles of Massinger's plays and the Sampson Agonistes are the two extremes of the arc within which the diction of dramatic poetry may oscillate. Shakspeare in his great plays is the midpoint."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a diction that fits the dramatic purpose — neither so colloquial it ceases to be poetic, nor so elevated it becomes implausible as speech. The effective middle ground (as in Shakespeare) preserves probability while retaining poetic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological plausibility; avoid exaggerated passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Massinger 'often deals in exaggerated passion' leading to actions (e.g., Malefort senior) that strain credibility; by contrast, Shakespeare supplies redeeming traits (Edmund) or leaves hideousness uncompromised (Regan/Goneril).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters' actions should be psychologically plausible; avoid over-exaggerated passions that would realistically lead to madness or incoherence. If a character performs extreme acts, provide believable motivation or redeeming traits to preserve credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of farce: grant an initial improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: "The definition of a farce is, an improbability or even impossibility granted in the outset, see what odd and laughable events will fairly follow from it!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For farce, establish an explicit improbable premise early and then rigorously explore logical or ludic consequences for comic effect. The audience's willing suspension of disbelief is secured by consistent consequence-drawing from the initial premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic artifice (disguise/unrecognized identities) can create fine scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: The old dramatists 'took great liberties...bringing parties in scene together, and representing one as not recognizing the other under some faint disguise. Some of their finest scenes are constructed on this ground.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devices like disguise and mistaken identity can generate powerful dramatic moments and comic/tragic effects when used skillfully. Use sparingly and with attention to dramatic plausibility and payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and condensation of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Shakespeare's 'extreme condensation which makes the couplets fall into epigrams' and the observation that dramatic couplets can be epigrammatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economy of language — condensed lines, epigrammatic couplets — can intensify impact. Strive for concise, potent phrasing that conveys layered meaning without verbosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous plotting is attainable and valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise of Ben Jonson's Alchemist as an example of a 'perfect' plot and Ben Jonson as 'intense and burning art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot — coherent, tightly-wrought, and purposeful — is a high artistic achievement; writers should aim for internal logic and structural rigor when the work's aims call for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama as a medium to blend poetic and philosophical aims
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the drama alone, as Shakspeare soon found out, could the sublime poet and profound philosopher find the conditions of a compromise."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use drama to synthesize lyrical/poetic expression with philosophical or intellectual exploration: stage action and dialogue can reconcile emotive and conceptual ambitions more readily than pure poetry or prose argument alone.
